items.question: How do you see the appeal of moving from physics into AI as a young researcher?

items.answer: I think many people who do physics, including Yao Shunyu, have had this kind of experience. items.question: How did your training in physics shape your response to the worst-case mathematical objection to developing the CAN network?

Their argument was that they had found a worst case. In that worst case, they could not find a strict two-layer smooth Kolmogorov-Arnold representation. That sounds long-winded; basically, it had a series of restrictive conditions in front of it. But as someone trained in physics, perhaps I sometimes do not care that much about what the worst case looks like. We care about typical cases: can it be useful in some settings? If it can, then it is a good thing. This may connect to the idea that all models are wrong but some are useful. So I thought: mathematically you tell me it does not work in the worst case, but in physics the things we care about have beautiful structure. They are not worst cases. Based on that optimism, I temporarily ignored Max’s warning that the 1989 paper said this did not work. I spent two weeks building the prototype, then went to Max and said, “Look, I trained this network.”

items.question: How did your desire to unify AI and physics shape your thinking about the CAN network?
items.object: The CAN network as a unification of neural networks and symbolic formulas
items.answer: I think this was a long-standing obsession of mine. I felt that the philosophies of AI and physics were too far apart. The philosophy of AI—at least current AI—is connectionist; it is neural. Physics, by contrast, is symbol-based. I felt it was bad for these two things not to be unified. Perhaps this comes from the impulse, after being trained in physics, to systematize and unify things. As early as 2021, I was thinking about how to construct a network that was both a network and a symbolic formula. It is a bit like wave-particle duality: in quantum physics, a particle is both a particle and a wave. Could I construct a network that was both a neural network and a symbolic formula? Based on that exploration, I wrote down such an equation. Only a few days later did I learn that the equation I wrote was in fact the equation Kolmogorov and Arnold had written in 1957. But I had arrived at it from another angle: the wave-particle duality between neural networks and symbolic formulas. Then I belatedly realized that two Soviet mathematicians had already written it in 1957, and had proved its universal approximation property—effectively giving our model theoretical backing: such a representation can represent any function. So in that sense, it closed out my long-standing obsession.

items.question: How did developing CAN change your thinking about how AI architectures should be designed?
items.object: CAN as a starting point for making AI model design a science
items.answer: CAN is more like an example for me. An example of what? That I, as a person, could design a new architecture by simply thinking it up. My mode of thinking is sometimes somewhat abstract, or high-level. After CAN succeeded, I was not thinking about how to apply CAN to different scenarios; I was thinking about how to reproduce this ability to propose new architectures. That led to my subsequent exploration of Physics of AI—the physics of AI. I think model design itself should be a science. It should not be that Transformers are thought up on the spot, GANs are thought up on the spot, ResNets are thought up on the spot, and CAN is thought up on the spot. That is very unscalable. I do not think we should scale compute or data; we should scale the design of AI models. But how do we scale that? That is another huge research question. So after CAN, it became a starting point for me. In a sense, I began thinking more about things that exist only in math and science: how did I think of it, and how can I distill my thinking process into a model? So it became my new obsession. It is also what AF_AI, the startup I am now involved in, wants to do: distill the mental circuitry of myself, or of the world’s top AI researchers, into a model. Or rather, not just distill it—I think it may even be able to produce things better than those produced by the very best human scientists and researchers.

items.question: How do you understand the role of language itself in the success of large language models?
items.object: Language and architecture in the success of large language models
items.answer: I agree quite strongly with a point Saining made in his previous interview with you: large language models are anti–Bitter Lesson. The reason LLMs can succeed is language; their success is not in the model. Language is a gift from nature, something humanity has evolved over millions of years. We take that gift and put a model on top of it; as long as the model can consume that gift, it is a good model. It may be a Transformer, but in a parallel universe it could be another model. We already have all kinds of variants, such as linear-attention models. For language models, I think architecture design here is comparatively less delicate, because language itself is already a well-compressed modality.

items.question: Why do you think model design will become more important in the post-LLM era?
items.object: Model design in the post-LLM era
items.answer: For many other modalities, such as vision—and I think this is also what many world-model companies are trying to solve—these modalities have not been compressed very well. At that point, it becomes very important how we construct a model that can compress. It is not merely a model that records all knowledge, as a Transformer does; it needs to learn abstract representations. This is what humans are best at, because there are simply too many variables in the world. For our ancestors, and for us, to survive, we needed to understand what mattered most for survival: there is fruit over there, I pick it and eat it, and I will not starve today; there is a tiger over there, and it must not find me. For evolutionary reasons, humans had to become especially good at identifying the most important parts of massive amounts of information. But this is precisely the kind of abstraction ability current AI does not yet have. Personally, that is why I think model design will become more important in the post-LLM era. The success of LLMs was not because of the model. Of course, saying this is a bit of hindsight, right? Transformers did have innovations: their attention mechanism lets information propagate rapidly across the context dimension, which prior models such as RNNs and LSTMs did not have. But if I find another model that also allows highly efficient information propagation across context, that model could be just as good as a Transformer. It is not great because it is called a Transformer; it is great because it enables efficient information propagation across context. Likewise, ResNet is not great because it is called ResNet; it is great because it enables efficient information propagation and gradient propagation along depth.

For our ancestors, and for us, to survive, we needed to understand what mattered most for survival: there is fruit over there, I pick it and eat it, and I will not starve today; there is a tiger over there, and it must not find me. For evolutionary reasons, humans had to become especially good at identifying the most important parts of massive amounts of information. Personally, that is why I think model design will become more important in the post-LLM era. The success of LLMs was not because of the model. Of course, saying this is a bit of hindsight, right? But if I find another model that also allows highly efficient information propagation across context, that model could be just as good as a Transformer. It is not great because it is called a Transformer; it is great because it enables efficient information propagation across context. Likewise, ResNet is not great because it is called ResNet; it is great because it enables efficient information propagation and gradient propagation along depth.

items.question: How do you understand the connection between your research goal of bridging the neural and symbolic worlds and AI for Science?
items.object: Bridging the neural and symbolic worlds through AI for Science
items.answer: The main thread is how to bridge the neural and symbolic worlds—or more specifically, how to bridge AI and physics, or more generally, the natural sciences. That is an ability given to us by the neural side. Overall, my research aims to bridge AI and science. items.question: What do you mean by AI for AI as a research direction?
items.object: AI for AI as a research direction
items.answer: With Science of AI, I am dissatisfied with AI as a black box. I am dissatisfied with AI as merely a neural thing. I want to use symbolic things, use science, to describe, understand, improve, and design this neural thing. That is Science of AI. So the AI for AI I mean is not completely the same as what people now call AI for AI. What people now call AI for AI may mean using a coding agent to write papers or improving their training pipeline. That still goes from neural to neural; it does not close the loop through the symbolic component. My AI for AI is about using automated methods to do the physics of AI: using AI to help us understand AI itself faster, and eventually closing the loop not only on understanding but on improving AI.

items.question: How has your understanding of the need for symbolic theories in the physics of AI evolved?
items.object: The role of symbolic theories in the physics of AI
items.answer: I think this partly depends on your belief. My belief is that AI is something half-physical and half-biological. Physics is—perhaps I can put it this way, as Elias Skinner said—“Intelligence is compression,” or conversely, “compression is intelligence.” I think symbols are an embodiment of extreme compression. When we can symbolize something, that means we can compress the data before us to an extreme degree. In scenarios like physics, we have that luxury: we can compress it into symbols. But perhaps in chemistry, biology, or more social sciences, we genuinely cannot symbolize it. So I think this is also an evolution in my understanding. For example, if you had asked me last year how to do the physics of AI, I would have said that it ultimately had to be symbolized. But as I have done more and more, I have realized that perhaps it is enough to make a predictor. Physics’s ultimate purpose is also prediction; I do not necessarily have to use a symbolic theory to make predictions. Once I have made a predictor, it can be neural—it can simply be a neural network. It does not have to be symbolic, as long as it is useful and predicts reasonably well in some scenarios. It can be neural. It is just that, so far, symbolic things remain a personal obsession of mine because they are more interpretable.

items.question: How do you use the history of astronomy to understand different levels of symbolic compression?
items.object: Astronomy as an example of levels of symbolic compression
items.answer: A favorite example of mine is astronomy, which has three stages. The first stage is Tycho: he observed the stars extensively and recorded which star was where at what time. That is the first stage, the data stage. The second stage is Kepler. Kepler fit planetary trajectories and discovered that they were elliptical. At that point, there were empirical formulas. The third stage is Newton. Newton took Kepler’s empirical formulas—Kepler’s three laws—and said, your three laws are still not fundamental; you need one more law. I will write down a formula for gravity, and I can predict all three of your laws. This is a typical process of compression. In Tycho’s era, you had to record the entire data table, which was highly inefficient. By Kepler’s era, an ellipse equation plus Kepler’s three laws could summarize the data well. Then in Newton’s era, Newton said, Kepler, this is still cumbersome; I can compress it further.

items.question: Where do you think current AI research stands in the progression from collecting observations to discovering fundamental laws?
items.object: AI’s scientific maturity and its concentration on Transformer architectures
items.answer: In current AI, we are roughly at—depending on how we measure it—what people sometimes call stage 1.5. What does that mean? We have a great many experiments, but not many empirical laws. Scaling laws, for example, are among the few empirical laws we know; they occupy a position similar to Kepler’s laws. We are still far from the Newton stage of AI. Of course, at other times I say, more pessimistically, perhaps we are actually at 0.5. Why? Tycho at least pointed a telescope at the sky and measured where stars were in each region. But we are now excessively focused on prematurely converging on architectures such as Transformers, and seem to have lost the motivation to explore other types of architectures. It is a little as if Tycho stared only at one region of the sky, became overly absorbed in it—wow, this region is so wonderful—and neglected observing the other regions. In that sense, perhaps we have not even reached the Tycho era, or even the age of data and big data. Our data only applies to Transformers and to a very small fraction of models. We are still far from the stage where we can see the entire sky.

items.question: How do you think AI for research can progress from its current early stage to automation at scale?
items.object: Structuring research so that AI can automate and scale it
items.answer:
I think some directions still need research; their paths are not completely clear yet. For example, the research we are doing here—AI for research, this Auto Research work—is not something with a fully clear route. It is actually very early. Of course, coding has already been very successful: AI for coding has been very successful. The next paradigm naturally becomes AI for research. But I believe research and coding are very different. Coding is highly structured, first of all. Second, it has a large amount of data. We already have GitHub, and the data on GitHub is much higher quality and much more structured than other parts of the internet. But research is not a well-structured data structure. We still often say we need research intuition and research taste. When we use those terms, we are implicitly acknowledging that research is not something that can be well structured. Once something can be structured, standardized, and scaled, people should become disenchanted with it. But we have not yet become disenchanted with research, which shows it has not yet been structured, standardized, or scaled.

What we need to do is the three steps I just mentioned. The first step is to structure research. When we do research ourselves, it may seem chaotic; our minds are chaotic—we jump from here to there—and those data have not been captured. In the future, we need to capture a structure for research: for example, we first observe something, a phenomenon; that phenomenon indicates what problem may exist in the system; we have a hypothesis about the problem; that hypothesis tells us what operation to perform next; and whether that operation really brings an improvement in training.

The abbreviation for our methodology is OPHIS: O-P-H-I-S. O is observation, P is problem, H is hypothesis, I is intervention, and S is speed up. We believe every research paper should be structured according to this framework. In the process of doing research, of course not all research proceeds smoothly as a single chain of thought like this; I may jump back and forth among different nodes. That is fine. But everything should at least be structured as O, P, H, I, or S. Once we have those structured things, we have in effect created a language of research. Of course, that sounds a bit mystical. I believe the language of research is broadly based on natural language, but its underlying structure requires us to abstract it ourselves and create this kind of structured language. Once we have a language of research, we can train a research-language language model just as we train a large language model. Then research can be automated and scaled. But the first step is to structure research.

items.answer: I think New Labs have identified some pain points in the current mainstream paradigm. Auto Research is one example. items.question: How did training yourself to predict model training curves lead you to the idea of AI for AI?
items.object: Developing intuition about model training through daily prediction experiments
items.answer: I think the recent idea of AI for AI was born when I began training myself as a model. This is something I began doing early this year: every day, I would randomly pick a dataset and randomly pick a model to train. Before doing the experiment, I would ask myself: predict what this training curve will look like. I did this day after day, for about sixty days, every day. If you look at my personal website, there is a blog column there, and you will find that in the early period I updated extremely frequently—every day, sometimes twice a day—because during that period I basically went into seclusion and trained myself as a model. After doing an experiment today, I would train my brain: this scenario, this model, this dataset, this optimizer, will produce this kind of training curve. At first my predictive ability was very poor; perhaps I could not even predict the trend correctly. But after training myself for roughly forty or fifty days, I found I began to get more accurate. Before doing an experiment, I could roughly predict what the result would look like. Sometimes, even if the experiment I did a few days earlier was language-related and the one I was doing today was vision-related, I could still predict it accurately.

items.question: How do you see language models helping automate AI research?
items.object: Language models as a technical route for AI for AI
items.answer: I think a language model is one technical route for AI for AI. Once you have a language model, it can do many things. For example, suppose you have one hundred ideas and do not know which one to try. More concretely, you have one hundred architectures and do not know which one to try. With a language model, you use the architecture as input to the language model, and it can predict what that model's performance will be like. Then you no longer need to run one hundred experiments. You only need to do one hundred forward passes through the language model and make one hundred predictions, which is very cheap. Of course, in the end we still need to actually run the experiment. But for screening ideas, a language model can help this AI-for-AI iterative system iterate on ideas faster. Previously, if you did not have good intuition and did not have a language model assisting you, then with, say, one hundred ideas, you might need to try them all. Now, the language model can rank them beforehand and tell you which ideas are more promising than the others. And the ideas here are more about doing AI research, so it is an AI-for-AI thing. I think AI for AI can sometimes sound a bit like a buzzword; sometimes I also call it auto research. But here, the research that we are automating is AI research. And the “auto” here is also being done with AI, so auto research is in fact also an AI-for-AI concept.

items.question: How do you approach building a meta-model that predicts other models’ training curves?
items.object: Building a meta-model that predicts other models’ training curves
items.answer: We will start with demos, because I think this is a relatively long-term, three-to-five-year undertaking. For our meta-model, our data are models. It is a bit convoluted here, because our meta-model is a model about models, or a world model about models. So our training data are models: we train these models and obtain their training curves. That gives us one data point. Then we generate another model, and that other model has a corresponding training curve. Once we have such pairs—model and training-curve pairs—we train this meta-model in a supervised way: when the input is this model, the meta-model should predict its training curve. That is how we train our meta-model. The expensive part is that we also need quite a lot of compute, but unlike large models, we do not need a huge cluster with excellent inter-GPU communication. Here, we need to build large numbers of small models. But by small models, we do not simply mean small Transformers. What we emphasize is diversity: we want this meta-model to have seen many architectures that look very strange to people, because perhaps such architectures can help us escape the current local minimum of Transformers.

items.question: How do you understand the role of “parallel universes” in Physics of AI?
items.object: Parallel universes, controlled experiments, and phase diagrams in Physics of AI
items.answer:
I think it is still because my PhD advisor Max Tegmark is one of the proponents of parallel-universe theory. Of course, “parallel universes” sounds mystical here; in fact, it simply means controlled experiments. For example, I have two Petri dishes, each with some bacteria, and the bacteria may be in different environments. To the bacteria in one Petri dish, the other dish is a parallel universe. In human scientific experiments, that corresponds to running controlled experiments. In one environment, what kind of model can I train? That environment may refer to how I set my hyperparameters. If I switch to another set of hyperparameters, I may obtain a model with different properties.

This is a very important methodology in Zhu Zeyuan's Physics of RLM: he sweeps out a phase diagram. Phase diagrams are also a common concept in physics. They mean that matter can take different forms and, under different conditions, have different phases. The same substance—H2O, water—can have different phases at different pressures and temperatures. There are also many phases in AI, whether in training dynamics or elsewhere. We often have know-how saying some trick works and some trick does not. But often that is phase-specific: a trick only works when your experiment is in that phase; when it leaves that phase and enters another one, that trick may stop working and another trick may work instead.

The reason we are so confused now is that everyone says, “My trick works,” but no one answers when it works—what phase their model or system needs to be in for it to work. This is also a problem that the science of AI, or physics of AI, wants to solve. We know from the no-free-lunch theorem that no model or trick can be better than all other methods on every dataset and every task. The task of Physics of AI is to clarify the conditions under which every trick and every architecture applies. That is a scientific attitude, rather than building something and selling it by saying, “Oh, ours is good,” while completely ignoring that it may only be good under certain conditions.

items.question: How do you understand interpretability as a goal of Physics of AI?
items.object: Interpretability as a goal of Physics of AI
items.answer: I am somewhat wary of the word “interpretability,” because different people now give it different interpretations. We see physics as explaining our natural world. So yes, I am doing interpretability; Physics of AI is doing interpretability. But how far does our interpretation need to go? We do not necessarily need to explain it down to the neuron level like Anthropic. Of course, from late 2022 through early 2024, we did a great deal of this kind of work. Because we did a great deal of work ourselves explaining what algorithms neural networks are implementing and understanding certain neurons, we came to realize that these stories are sometimes not that robust. Broadly speaking, it can be called interpretability, but that does not necessarily mean we must reach the level of mechanistic interpretability like Anthropic.

items.answer: With this AutoRL thing we are doing, we hope to start more from first principles, from something more symbolic. Why do I say “more symbolic”? I previously coined a term myself: structuralism. I would say this is a form of structuralism. The reason I do not call it symbolism is that there are too many symbolism haters. If I say we are symbolic, people say, “Boring, boring—an antique.” But I think symbolism and connectionism have historically swung back and forth continuously; we need to break out of that.

items.question: How do you assess Anthropic’s approach to understanding the internal workings of AI models?
items.object: Anthropic’s approach to mechanistic interpretability
items.answer: I think Anthropic is relatively extreme and aggressive: they say they can understand what an individual neuron is doing. Perhaps one neuron is, for example, a profanity neuron; if I shut that neuron off, it will not use profanity. But examples like this are very unstable. You may find such a neuron in one example, but after changing the random seed, that behavior may not exist in that network. Their series of work, including sparse autoencoders and transcoders, is based on this idea: that I can lift mixed internal representations—representations in superposition—into a higher-dimensional but very sparse space, so that some atomic concepts within them can be extracted. But personally I think there is some wishful thinking in this. I still respect them greatly, because in late 2022 and early 2023, when we were doing mechanistic interpretability, we took the same approach, so we know some of the weaknesses in it. People on their interpretability team, including Samuel Marks and Vasco Ni, as well as an undergraduate I previously supervised at MIT, all eventually went to Anthropic; they also came out of our group early on. For example, Vasco Ni's work at Anthropic on how Claude does addition was also an extension of a paper from our group. So after I took off my scholar's robe, I came to feel that these are all very interesting stories. But what's beyond that? That is something I have also been thinking about.

items.question: How has the prospect of automated research changed your view of mechanistic interpretability?
items.object: Mechanistic interpretability under the AFAI framework
items.answer: Recently I have begun reconsidering mechanistic interpretability. I think it is because, under this new AFAI framework, mechanistic interpretability suddenly no longer feels so elusive. This is similar to my earlier judgment about the physics of AI: mechanistic interpretability is somewhat like the biology of AI. I previously thought that biology has been developing for a long time, medicine has been developing for so long, so the biology of AI and mechanistic interpretability would also need several hundred years to develop. Again, returning to the AFAI framework, I think the reason it would need hundreds or thousands of years is that we have no way to automate it. Once we can automate it, progress can actually be very fast. Recently I saw Professor Tang Jie say that Zhipu will invest trillion-level resources in mechanistic interpretability. If I had seen that half a year ago, I would have thought: what are they doing? But now, placed in the AFAI framework, I think mechanistic interpretability is indeed a good goal. I previously found it unpromising because it was simply too difficult. It is the same with the physics of AI: it is a good goal, but because it is so difficult, it used to feel very frustrating. But now, with auto-research—at least we are building it; it does not exist yet—once we have this auto-research system, I think these North Star goals that previously seemed so inexplicable and distant may actually be attainable within three to five years.

items.question: What would you consider a convincing demonstration of an AFAI system's ability to propose a new architecture?
items.object: AFAI's standard for a convincing new architecture
items.answer: I still think of Kaiming: why did everyone use Kaiming's ResNet? Some say it was very elegant, but let us not forget that on ImageNet, Kaiming was ten percentage points ahead of second place. So I think: either you knock your opponent out with your fists, or if you cannot knock them out with your fists, then you need words to persuade them—you persuade with reason. This AFAI system should be able to propose a new architecture in a vertical domain. And the new architecture should be able to top the leaderboard—not by gaining one percentage point, but by gaining ten percentage points.

items.question: Why do you see auto-research, or AFAI, as necessary but insufficient for AGI?
items.object: Auto-research, or AFAI, as a step toward AGI
items.answer: I think all of these terms are somewhat fuzzy. I think it is necessary, but not sufficient. I think one more thing is missing—the thing we have been discussing: abstracting data. I think abstraction is important because humans have continual learning ability, and humans have continual learning ability because they can abstract. But current AI still cannot abstract. If it can abstract, it is at most because the data themselves have already been abstracted, as with natural language. So I think that to achieve true AGI, in addition to AFAI, it needs an ability to abstract; and the ability to abstract is a necessary ability for continual learning. It depends on whether our definition of AFAI requires it to have continual learning ability. Because it sounds like when you stack the word AI, it steps on its own foot and flies into the sky. When I say it needs continual learning ability, perhaps my definition of AFAI is more pragmatic: it can propose a good architecture in a vertical domain. To achieve that goal, you do not actually need to solve continual learning. But to solve AGI, you definitely need to solve continual learning.

items.question: How do you envision the training autopilot you want to build?
items.object: A training autopilot as the product behind AI research
items.answer: I think that in conversations with investors, we gradually clarified what the product would ultimately look like. Because language models and the physics of AI, after all this discussion, are still technologies. Ultimately, the question is: technology behind what product? The product we ultimately want to build is a training autopilot. In the shorter term, it will be a training copilot. What does that mean? Not everyone today has the ability to train models, but in the future everyone could train their own private model. That private model does not necessarily have to be an LM, though perhaps it is fine-tuned from an LM. A user only needs to tell our system what their requirements are, and our system can end-to-end design the model, train the model, deploy the model, and deliver it to them for direct use. Importantly, the user can say, “I only have one hundred dollars.” Within that budget, you should deliver the best model possible. Ultimately, if such a system can do this end-to-end, it is actually quite similar to things like CloudCode and vibe coding today. The difference is that today the target user is a programmer: I want to do a particular task, and you generate the code. In the future, it will be a more closed-loop thing. I would not even need to tell you the technical route. I would not tell you to use a Transformer, or how to train it. I would only tell you what I need. Then I can end-to-end design, train, and deploy the model for you.

items.question: What do you think a system that automatically designs, trains, and deploys AI models based on users’ requirements could make possible?
items.object: Accessible, end-to-end AI model training, or “vibe training”
items.answer:
The point is that people do not train their own models now because the barrier is too high. Once that capability exists and we make the cost-performance ratio high enough, people will have that need. For example, suppose I buy a robot dog to keep me company. I might want to save some of my data—my voice data and records of conversations with it—to help train it, whether through fine-tuning or something else, so that the robot dog can make me happier. For example, rather than just barking “woof, woof, woof” all day, it can also say things to comfort me. Today, no one would say that, in order to make something like that, they are going to learn to train things themselves. Of course, some startups may now have similar ideas.

But what we envision for the future is that, with this system, we are not ourselves building one OpenAI; it can incubate an OpenAI for every industry and vertical domain. When I say vertical domains, I am already speaking at a level above language models: our language model—though it need not necessarily be a language model—the ultimate system can design these Transformer-like models for every vertical domain. Just as LMs unified the various tasks in NLP, natural-language processing, we now build different models for different tasks. People building world models build world models; people building LMs build LMs; people building an AI-for-science model build an AI-for-science model. But these domains are still generally not interconnected.

But in the future there will be such a God—something for vibe training. Right now it is vibe coding; in the future it will be vibe training. You state your requirements clearly, and it can end-to-end design, train, and deploy the model for you. Once we have this capability—well, to be honest, I have not thought it through either—what needs will exist for every user to train their own model. But often, when technology becomes cheap enough, needs emerge naturally. It is just that we have not reached that point yet, so it is hard to imagine it.

items.question: How do you assess RSI's approach to automated AI research?
items.object: RSI's approach to automated AI research
items.answer: As for RSI, we do not really know, but we can glimpse some of their technical route from their blog. We roughly guess that they emphasize maintaining good memory in an auto-research system. For example, if I ran five experiments yesterday, all adjusting the learning rate, and all five failed, then today I remember those experiments and will not keep adjusting the learning rate. But again, maintaining a good memory system does not mean you understand why the learning rate failed. Your earlier experience may not necessarily be correct: perhaps the learning-rate failures before were due to reason A, but when I run an experiment the next day, the reason may actually be B, and adjusting the learning rate may then be the right thing. So there remains the question of whether it is merely experience-driven or mechanism-driven. Of course, based on their website, and because Professor Tian Yuandong is there, I believe they will also invest to some extent in the science of AI. But at present it is still not particularly clear what their science-of-AI route is.

items.question: How do you understand the reasoning behind what researchers call taste or intuition?
items.object: Research taste, intuition, and the reasoning behind moments of insight
items.answer: I think every moment of insight definitely has a chain of thought. If not, you have not questioned yourself deeply enough. My own experience is this: at first I also rather believed in research taste and research intuition, but I have now somewhat demystified them. I think research taste and intuition are actually a fig leaf: we are smart enough to come up with an idea, but not smart enough to explain in language how we came up with it. So we call insight “taste,” “intuition,” or a flash of inspiration. There is also a saying: “The skilled fighter has no dazzling achievements.” It means that for the very best people, proposing ideas is as easy as breathing. Things that others find astonishing—“Wow, how did they think of that?”—they can systematically turn into their own system. People who are not at the very top can also propose some very good ideas, but they may not know how they came up with them. I have intentionally trained myself to do this: not only to come up with good ideas, but also to ask how I came up with them. In the process, I am trying to put my ideas into language. This is actually very difficult for me, because I am not someone who communicates particularly smoothly through natural language. My mode of thought may be more like Max Tegmark, my PhD advisor: we are both very visual.

There is another route, of course: when neuroscience has developed sufficiently, and we have no ethical issues—for example, if we can measure a person's brain waves invasively, or have more advanced non-invasive methods that can obtain fairly clear brain-wave signals—then I do not need language; I can simply measure that person's brain waves. But then I need that person's brain waves. Since we currently cannot obtain people's brain waves, we can only interrogate them, or interrogate ourselves: how exactly did I come up with that idea just now? If you cannot say it, that means you have not interrogated yourself deeply enough. As long as you interrogate deeply enough, you can always say something. It may not fully replace the value of brain waves, but at least you can say something.

items.question: Why do you think a new lab needs six to twelve months of R&D before committing to commercialization?
items.object: R&D and commercialization timing for a new lab
items.answer: For the next six months, we will still focus on R&D: building demos and some initial product prototypes. After six months, we will decide what to do next based on the results of those six months. We will definitely start productization and commercialization around the one-year mark. But I think six to twelve months of research and development is very important for a new lab. You cannot invest too early in a direction that is not actually that good merely in order to deliver something in the short term or commercialize in the short term. You need six to twelve months of exploration to find a better direction.

items.answer: Personally, I think the route is now relatively clear. I think we can put a comma after six to twelve months and begin building a product. items.question: How do you understand the limitations of large language models in world modeling and Auto Research?
items.object: Large language models, world models, and Auto Research
items.answer: They cannot reach them, but the reason is not that I am a Transformer hater. I think it is more that on the world-model side, we need to find a much newer architecture that can better abstract and find the true latent space of the physical world. On the Auto Research side, I think it is more that large language models have not seen this kind of data. So the first step is structuring it, and the second is collecting this kind of structured research data. That is the most important thing. Once we have these data, large models can consume them too, and may do quite well. Of course, the meta-model route is a model about models. Large models also perform poorly because they have not seen data about models, or very much structured data about models.

items.question: How do you see the challenge of becoming an entrepreneur while continuing your technical research?
items.object: The experience of becoming an entrepreneur while doing technical research
items.answer: Basically, aside from sleeping, I am working all the time. But I think it is also quite a new experience. On the one hand, you have more resources and meet more people; it is as if you suddenly gain access to a bigger world. But on the other hand, you still have to do the technical and research work solidly and conscientiously. It is quite a challenge. Before, it was simply a matter of doing research conscientiously. But now, beyond doing the research at hand, you have to communicate with many people. And you have to think not only about the present but also about years ahead, work backward from the goals years ahead, and determine what route we should take. So I think this is somewhat out of my distribution, and it is something I am learning.

items.question: How do you think research and commercialization should be sequenced when building a company around Auto Research or World Models?
items.object: Research-driven company building for Auto Research and World Models
items.answer: I think it still depends on whether the thing being done needs to be research-driven early on. For Auto Research and World Models, I think at least six to twelve months of research-driven time is needed. That period cannot be skipped. Then, for example, after six to twelve months, when I have turned what is in my head into a demo—into a prototype that I can see in front of me—we can bring in co-founders with product and commercialization experience to help expand its impact, rather than leaving it merely a small but beautiful thing. But I think the first requirement is six to twelve months to build the prototype.

items.question: How did reading Sapiens change your understanding of society?
items.object: Sapiens
items.answer: Sapiens, probably. I have always been rather nerdy and not very knowledgeable about social science.
